claims.text: A thin nickel interlayer combined with directional solidification will enhance bonding at the W–Cu interface.
Nickel is an example of a refractory-metal interlayer suitable for this intervention.
Directional solidification of the coated precursor will produce continuous, aligned copper lamellae.
A cooling rate of approximately 10–20 °C/s is suitable for producing the proposed W–Cu structure.
Under the proposed directional thermal conditions, copper will melt and segregate into an aligned phase while tungsten remains solid.
A gradient furnace or modified spark-plasma-sintering setup can provide the directional heating and cooling required by the proposed process.
The interlayer will promote chemical compatibility between tungsten and copper during solidification.
The resulting composite will contain well-bonded, continuous copper lamellae aligned with heat flow and coupled to a continuous tungsten matrix.
The interlayer improves W–Cu wettability during directional solidification.
Continuous copper networks reduce electron scattering and thereby facilitate thermal transport.
The tungsten framework will maintain the composite's mechanical integrity.
The tungsten framework will maintain irradiation resistance.
The engineered composite will have approximately 20–30% higher thermal conductivity than a conventionally processed isotropic W–Cu composite.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a significant loss of mechanical durability.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a significant loss of irradiation resistance under fusion-reactor joint conditions.
The benefits will persist under high heat-flux conditions if processing provides adequate phase separation and interfacial integrity.
Uniform interlayer application and avoidance of unwanted interfacial phases are potential process risks.

The hypothesis is to be falsified if the interlayer sample achieves less than a 20% thermal-conductivity increase over the directional-solidification control or suffers significant losses in durability or irradiation resistance.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline and predicted comparison use a conventional isotropic W–Cu composite, whereas the falsification experiment uses a directionally solidified composite without an interlayer. This control isolates the interlayer but does not test the full combined intervention against the stated baseline.
